content: Mechanical methods were the first techniques developed to prepare the cervix and induce labor. Over the past few decades, these methods have largely been replaced by pharmacological approaches. However, mechanical methods may offer certain advantages, such as a reduction in side effects, which could lead to improved neonatal outcomes. This review updates previous analyses published in 2001 and 2012. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of mechanical methods for inducing labor in the third trimester (after 24 weeks of gestation) compared to pharmacological methods, including prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) administered vaginally or intracervically, low-dose misoprostol (oral or vaginal), amniotomy, or oxytocin. Mechanical methods for labor induction include: 1. Insertion of a catheter through the cervix into the extra-amniotic space, followed by balloon inflation. 2. Placement of laminaria tents or synthetic equivalents (e.g., Dilapan) into the cervical canal. 3. Use of a catheter to inject fluid into the extra-amniotic space (extra-amniotic saline infusion, or EASI). The review compared these mechanical methods to pharmacological methods, including: 1. Balloon catheters, laminaria tents, or EASI versus prostaglandins (various types and routes) or oxytocin. 2. Single-balloon catheters versus double-balloon catheters. 3. Mechanical methods combined with prostaglandins or oxytocin versus prostaglandins or oxytocin alone. The review included 112 trials, with data from 104 studies involving 22,055 women and 21 different comparisons. The quality of evidence ranged from very low to moderate, with many studies downgraded due to lack of blinding and imprecise effect estimates. Key Findings: 1. Balloon Catheter vs. Vaginal PGE2: There may be little or no difference in the likelihood of vaginal delivery not being achieved within 24 hours (risk ratio [RR] 1.01, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.82 to 1.26; low-quality evidence). There is probably little or no difference in cesarean section rates (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.09; moderate-quality evidence). Balloon catheters probably reduce the risk of uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate (FHR) changes (RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.67; moderate-quality evidence). They also likely reduce the risk of serious neonatal morbidity or perinatal death (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.93; moderate-quality evidence). There may be a slight reduction in neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admissions (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.04; low-quality evidence). It is uncertain whether there is a difference in serious maternal morbidity or death (RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.01 to 4.12; very low-quality evidence) or in five-minute Apgar scores below 7 (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.14; low-quality evidence). 2. Balloon Catheter vs. Low-Dose Vaginal Misoprostol: It is uncertain whether there is a difference in vaginal deliveries not achieved within 24 hours (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.39; low-quality evidence). Balloon catheters probably reduce the risk of uterine hyperstimulation with FHR changes (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.85; moderate-quality evidence). However, they may increase the risk of cesarean sections (RR 1.28, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.60; low-quality evidence). It is uncertain whether there is a difference in serious neonatal morbidity or perinatal death (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.12 to 2.66; very low-quality evidence), serious maternal morbidity or death (no events; very low-quality evidence), five-minute Apgar scores below 7 (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.97; low-quality evidence), or NICU admissions (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.63; low-quality evidence). 3. Balloon Catheter vs. Low-Dose Oral Misoprostol: Balloon catheters probably increase the risk of vaginal delivery not being achieved within 24 hours (RR 1.28, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.46; moderate-quality evidence). They also probably slightly increase the risk of cesarean sections (RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.32; moderate-quality evidence). It is uncertain whether there is a difference in uterine hyperstimulation with FHR changes (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.38; low-quality evidence), serious neonatal morbidity or perinatal death (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.60 to 2.06; low-quality evidence), serious maternal morbidity or death (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.05 to 5.52; very low-quality evidence), five-minute Apgar scores below 7 (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.32; low-quality evidence), or NICU admissions (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.17; low-quality evidence). Authors' Conclusions: Moderate-quality evidence suggests that mechanical induction with a balloon catheter is likely as effective as vaginal PGE2 for labor induction, with a more favorable safety profile. Further research on this comparison may not be necessary. Moderate-quality evidence indicates that balloon catheters may be slightly less effective than oral misoprostol, but the safety outcomes for neonates remain unclear. Low-quality evidence suggests that balloon catheters may be less effective than low-dose vaginal misoprostol but likely have a better safety profile. Future research should focus on neonatal safety and maternal satisfaction.
